world_behind.title: A chapter of quoted speech
world_behind.text: More than a dozen sentences here are things people will say, given in their own words: I am the Lord's, there is no God today, eat and drink, all is well, we have enough. Nephi's method in this chapter is to let a future age convict itself out of its own mouth.

world_behind.title: Churches that contend
world_behind.text: Verses 3 and 4 describe competing religious bodies whose priests argue with each other and teach with their learning. Nephi's colony had no such landscape. He is describing a market in religion, which is a specific historical condition rather than a general failing.

world_behind.title: A few stripes
world_behind.text: The reasoning in verse 8 ends with an expected sentence: beaten with a few stripes, and saved at last. Corporal punishment by a fixed count was ordinary in Israelite law, capped at forty. What the verse imagines is not lawlessness but a defendant who has read the penalty schedule and finds it affordable.

world_behind.title: Robbing the poor with buildings
world_behind.text: Verse 13 names fine sanctuaries and fine clothing as the mechanism of the robbery. Ancient temples were also treasuries, and the charge is that religious display is paid for out of what the poor needed. The accusation is economic and concrete.

world_behind.title: Two devils, two methods
world_behind.text: Verses 20 through 22 divide the opposition's tactics: rage in some hearts, and in others a lulling into security, flattery, and the claim that there is no hell and no devil. The second is given more space, and it is the one the chapter's woes are aimed at.

world_behind.title: A quiet promise at the end
world_behind.text: After thirty-one verses of warning, verse 32 says the arm is lengthened out day to day and that God will be merciful, even to those who deny him. The chapter, like the Babylon oracle earlier in this book, refuses to end on the sentence.

words.text: A rule taught by an authority. The word runs through the chapter five times, and it is always contested: our precept against my precepts, the precepts of men against precepts given by the power of the Holy Ghost. Nephi does not object to precepts. He objects to whose they are.

Inflated with air, and therefore larger than the substance inside it. The word appears three times in four verses, applied to churches, to hearts, and to the wise and rich. It is the block's height vocabulary carried into Nephi's own prose, and the image adds emptiness to elevation.

To soothe into sleep, the verb used of a child. It is the chapter's most disquieting word because nothing about it is violent. The devil in verse 21 does not attack anyone; he calms them, and the result is carnal security, which is a phrase for being comfortable in the wrong place.

Tells people what pleases them. Paired with lulling, it completes a picture of opposition by agreement rather than by argument. What the flattery says is that there is no hell and no devil, which means the most effective lie in the chapter is one that makes the liar disappear.

Comfort, freedom from trouble, and here it is the subject of a wo. Being at ease in Zion is not named as a sin of commission at all; the condition itself is the charge. Set beside the lulling of verse 21, ease is what the sleep feels like from inside.

phrases.text: The doubled pronoun is the whole characterization. Two churches say the same sentence at each other, each stressing the first word, and neither is quoted saying anything about God. Nephi could have described sectarian rivalry in the abstract. Instead he gives it one line of dialogue and lets it repeat.

phrases.term: the Lord and the Redeemer hath done his work
phrases.text: The argument attributed to future teachers is not that God never existed but that he has finished. It is a doctrine of completion: revelation happened, miracles happened, and both are over. The chapter's answer arrives twenty-five verses later as line upon line, which is a claim that the work is still being done.

phrases.term: Eat, drink, and be merry, for tomorrow we die
phrases.text: An old saying, quoted by Isaiah against Jerusalem's fatalists and by Paul as the position of people who do not believe in resurrection: "let us eat and drink; for to morrow we die" (1 Cor. 15:32). Nephi puts it in the mouth of one group and then, in the next verse, in the mouth of a second group who add fear God to it, which is the stranger combination.

phrases.term: he will justify in committing a little sin
phrases.text: The doctrine of the manageable amount. The verse spells out the practice, lie a little, take advantage, dig a pit, and then the expected outcome, a few stripes and salvation at last. Nothing in it denies God, judgment, or the atonement. It simply treats them as priced, and Nephi's wo falls on the arithmetic rather than on the appetite.

phrases.term: the blood of the saints shall cry from the ground
phrases.text: The figure comes from the first murder, where a brother's blood cries from the ground, and the record has already used voices from the dust for its own coming forth two chapters running. Here the ground speaks in accusation instead. The same earth that holds the buried book holds the buried witnesses.

phrases.term: they rob the poor because of their fine sanctuaries
phrases.text: Said twice in one verse with two objects, sanctuaries and clothing, and the verb is rob rather than neglect. Nephi is not describing indifference to the poor but a transfer: what the buildings and the robes cost came from somewhere. The verse then adds persecution of the meek, so the poor lose twice.

The chapter's most quoted line, and its setting is worth keeping. It is not a hymn or a confession; it is what people say after being lulled and pacified, and the sentence immediately after it says the devil cheats their souls. The words themselves are unobjectionable, which is precisely why they work.

phrases.term: I am no devil, for there is none
phrases.text: The flattery's content, and it is self-erasing. Nephi's opposition does his best work by denying his own existence, which makes verse 22 the chapter's sharpest piece of characterization. The whispering is described as continuing until the chains are already on.

phrases.term: We have received, and we need no more
phrases.text: Repeated in expanded form two verses later about the word of God specifically. The wo does not fall on people who reject scripture but on people who are content with the scripture they have. In a chapter addressed to readers holding a new book, the placement is not accidental.

phrases.term: built upon the rock, receiving it with gladness
phrases.text: The test is emotional rather than intellectual. New truth arrives, and one person is glad while another trembles and is angry. The Sermon on the Mount uses the same two foundations for houses in a storm; Nephi applies them to the reception of a message, which makes the storm an idea.

phrases.term: line upon line, precept upon precept
phrases.text: Isaiah used the phrase mockingly, quoting drunkards imitating a prophet's tedious teaching, "precept upon precept; line upon line" (Isa. 28:10). Nephi turns the mockery into God's stated method and attaches a blessing to those who hearken. What was a complaint about how slowly revelation comes becomes the description of how it comes at all.

phrases.term: Cursed is he that putteth his trust in man
phrases.text: The block's last verse warned its hearers to cease from man, whose breath is in his nostrils. Nephi's own prose now states it as a curse and adds the exception that matters: unless their precepts are given by the power of the Holy Ghost. He is not against listening to people. He is against taking a rule on without ever asking where it came from.

verses.label: v. 3–6
verses.title: Rival churches, and a finished God
verses.text: Two claims are put in future mouths: that each body is the Lord's, and that God has completed his work and no longer does miracles. The two go together. A God who has finished cannot settle an argument between churches, which leaves learning and contention to do it.

verses.label: v. 7–9
verses.title: Three positions on a little sin
verses.text: Eat and drink because death is coming; eat and drink but fear God, who will allow a small account; teach this as doctrine and hide the counsel. The passage moves from appetite to theology to institution in three verses, and the last one is where the wo attaches.

verses.label: v. 11–14
verses.title: The diagnosis, and the exception
verses.text: All gone out of the way, corrupted, lifted up, puffed up, robbing, persecuting, stiff necks and high heads. Then verse 14 names the exception, a few humble followers of Christ, and immediately says even they are led astray in many instances. Nephi will not let the remnant be a comfortable category.

verses.label: v. 15–19
verses.title: A sentence interrupted
verses.text: The wo falls on the wise, learned, rich, false teachers, and those who turn aside the just. Then verse 17 interrupts the sentence: if they repent they will not be destroyed. The kingdom of the devil must shake, and even that shaking is described as stirring people up to repentance.

verses.label: v. 20–23
verses.title: Two methods, described in order
verses.text: Rage first, in one verse; then pacifying, lulling, flattering, whispering, across three. The proportion tells the reader which one Nephi thinks does more damage. The passage ends with the chains already on and a judgment scene, and the transition from whisper to chain has no visible moment.

verses.label: v. 24–29
verses.title: Six woes on comfort
verses.text: At ease, crying all is well, hearkening to the precepts of men, denying the power of God, saying we have received enough, trembling at truth. Every one of them is a posture rather than an act. Nobody in this list is doing anything; they are settled.

verses.label: v. 30–32
verses.title: The positive doctrine, at last
verses.text: Line upon line as God's stated way of teaching, a curse on trusting in man with an exception for the Spirit, and then the Gentiles warned and promised mercy in the same verse. Three verses hold the chapter's entire positive doctrine after twenty-nine of diagnosis.

chapter.title: Comfort is the adversary here
chapter.text: Rage appears in one verse. Everything else in the second half is soothing: pacified, lulled, flattered, at ease, all is well, we have enough. Nephi's account of how people are lost in the last days involves no persecution and very little temptation. It is a description of falling asleep.

chapter.title: The woes fall on settled positions
chapter.text: Read the list in verses 24 through 29 and notice that not one of them names a deed. Being at ease, saying all is well, preferring men's precepts, needing no more. The chapter treats a fixed state of mind as the thing worth six woes, which is unusual in scripture and specific to this subject.

chapter.title: A book about a book
chapter.text: Verse 2 says what is written out of the book will be of great worth, and verse 27 pronounces a wo on those who say they need no more of the word of God. Nephi is describing the reception of the very volume his readers are holding, and he knows the objection it will meet before it exists.

chapter.title: One sentence answers all of it
chapter.text: Against a God who has finished his work, against precepts of men, against having enough already, Nephi puts one sentence: line upon line, precept upon precept, here a little and there a little. The doctrine is not argued. It is stated as God's own method and blessed.

chapter.title: Everyone is quoted
chapter.text: The chapter's rhetorical strategy is citation. Nephi rarely says what people will believe; he says what they will say, in their words, and the sentences are ordinary enough to be recognizable. That is what makes the chapter uncomfortable rather than merely severe.

chapter.title: It ends where the Babylon oracle ended
chapter.text: Mercy, offered to the people just condemned, in the last verse. Two Nephi does this repeatedly, and it is worth noticing as a habit of the book rather than a feature of one chapter: the sentence is never the last word.

applications.title: Find yourself in the dialogue
applications.text: The chapter works by putting sentences in people's mouths. Write the sentence you actually say about your own standing before God, in your words, and see whether it appears anywhere in verses 3 through 9.

applications.title: Price the little sin honestly
applications.text: The position Nephi names is a calculation, not an appetite. Identify the thing you allow because you have decided it is small, and articulate the arithmetic you are using. Seeing it written is usually enough.

applications.title: Trace one line of spending
applications.text: The charge is that fine buildings and fine clothing come out of the poor. Look at one thing you have bought for appearance in a religious or professional context, and ask what else that money was available for.

applications.title: Test for lulling, not for temptation
applications.text: Ask where you are most comfortable in your spiritual life, and then ask whether that comfort is peace or sedation. The chapter's diagnostic is not guilt; it is ease.

applications.title: Say what you still need
applications.text: The wo falls on those who have enough. Name one thing you do not yet understand or have not yet received, out loud, and go looking for it this week.

applications.title: Watch your reaction to new truth
applications.text: Next time you encounter a correction or an unfamiliar teaching, note your first physical reaction. Gladness and trembling are the chapter's two foundations, and the test happens before you have decided anything.

applications.title: Check the source of a precept
applications.text: Take one rule you live by that came from a person. Ask whether you have ever tested it against the Spirit, and be willing to keep it or drop it on that basis rather than on who said it.

questions.text: Do I actually expect God to act today, or do I believe in a finished work?
What is my version of "a little sin," and when did I decide the price?
Whose expense is my respectability paid at?
If I am at ease, is it because things are well or because I have stopped looking?
What would I have to admit I need in order to stop saying I have enough?
When truth arrives uninvited, do I receive it with gladness or with anger?
Do I believe the mercy in this verse extends to the people I have written off?
